findings.title: Backup code login can skip password verification entirely
findings.body: In the credentials `authorize` callback, the password check at line 121 is gated on `!credentials.totpCode`, and the new backup-code branch at line 131 verifies only the backup code. A crafted request to the credentials callback containing a valid `backupCode` together with any non-empty dummy `totpCode` therefore skips `verifyPassword` and is authenticated solely by the backup code — a static, 40-bit secret that users store in files/notes. Backup codes are meant to substitute for the authenticator as the second factor, not to replace the password, so a leaked backup code alone yields full account access. The password should be verified (when the user has one) before accepting a backup code, or the flow branching should be keyed off the presence of `backupCode` instead of piggybacking on the `totpCode` gate.

findings.title: missing_backup_codes message directs users to a settings option that does not exist
findings.body: The new string `missing_backup_codes` reads "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.", but this PR adds no way to generate or regenerate backup codes outside the initial 2FA setup. Every user who enabled 2FA before this feature shipped has `backupCodes = null`; if they lose their authenticator and use the new "Lost access" link at login, they hit `MissingBackupCodes` and are told to do something impossible — they cannot log in to reach settings, and even in settings there is no regeneration option. These users are effectively locked out (admin intervention required). Either add a regeneration flow or change the message.

findings.title: No test exercises the actual backup-code authentication behavior
findings.body: The only test additions assert that the download/copy/close buttons render on the post-enable screen. Nothing tests the security-critical behavior of the feature: logging in with a backup code, that a redeemed code is invalidated and cannot be reused, that the password is still required alongside a backup code (see the related finding on password skipping), or disabling 2FA with a backup code. The added TODO comment ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup") and the unchecked PR checklist item concede this. For an authentication feature, the login-with-backup-code and single-use-invalidation paths should be covered before merge.

findings.title: Backup code redemption is a non-atomic read-modify-write
findings.body: The login flow decrypts the stored codes, checks `indexOf`, and then writes the updated array back in a separate `prisma.user.update`. Two concurrent sign-in requests presenting the same backup code can both decrypt and pass `indexOf` before either update commits, so a code intended to be single-use can be redeemed twice. Use a transaction with a conditional update (or a per-code consumed flag updated atomically) so only one request can consume a given code.

findings.title: Consumed backup codes are nulled instead of removed
findings.body: After a successful redemption the code does `backupCodes[index] = null` and re-encrypts the array, so the stored value permanently accumulates null placeholders (e.g. `[null, null, "abc123...", ...]`). Single-use still works because `indexOf` no longer matches the redeemed string, but the stored blob grows with junk entries and reveals exactly how many codes have been used. Splice the element out (or filter nulls) before re-encrypting.

findings.title: Backup codes stored with reversible encryption instead of hashing
findings.body: Backup codes are stored via `symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes), CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`. Unlike the TOTP secret, the stored codes are never read back for display — the one-time display uses the in-memory values returned by this same endpoint, and login/disable only need an equality check — so they could be stored as one-way hashes (like passwords). As implemented, anyone who obtains both the database and the encryption key recovers every user's unused backup codes in cleartext.

findings.title: Dismissing the dialog on the backup-codes step loses the codes with no recovery path
findings.body: The backup codes are shown exactly once on the `DisplayBackupCodes` step, and only the explicit Close button calls `onEnable()`. If the user dismisses the dialog at this step in any other way (ESC key or the dialog's close control, which fire `onOpenChange`), the modal closes without `onEnable` being called and the codes — which exist only in this component's React state — can never be displayed or regenerated again. The user's only recourse is to disable and re-enable 2FA. Consider intercepting dismissal on this step with a warning, or providing a way to regenerate codes later.

findings.title: Copy button shows a success toast even when the clipboard write fails
findings.body: The copy handler calls `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` without awaiting or catching it, then immediately fires `showToast(t("backup_codes_copied"), "success")`. In non-secure contexts or when clipboard permission is denied, `writeText` rejects (an unhandled promise rejection) while the user is told the codes were copied — they may close the dialog believing they have codes they don't. Await the promise and only show the success toast on fulfillment, with an error toast on rejection.

findings.title: Backup codes unusable in the SAML/Google TOTP login flow
findings.body: When a user with 2FA logs in via Google/SAML they are redirected to `/auth/login?totp=<jwt>` (`totpEmail` set), and in that state the footer renders `ExternalTotpFooter`, which only offers Cancel — there is no "Lost access" option, so these users cannot enter a backup code even though the credentials provider would accept one. Accounts that enabled 2FA and later moved to an identity-provider login (e.g. after linking Google, which nulls the password) have no self-service recovery path if they lose their authenticator.

findings.title: Password visibility toggle removed from keyboard tab order
findings.body: Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button removes it from keyboard navigation in every `PasswordField` across the app, while it keeps only an sr-only label. Keyboard and screen-reader users can no longer reach the control to verify what they typed. If the goal was to streamline tab order, this trades away an accessibility affordance; consider leaving it focusable.
